utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you, Mr. Oric. Are you receiving interpretation in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I am receiving interpretation and I fully understand the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My name is Jan Wubben.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with the co-counsels Ms. Joanne Richardson, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us here today are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Now, before we bring any witness, any preliminaries? Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then may I ask a question. I am informed that yesterday or the day before yesterday, rather, you gave us a courtesy copy of a motion relating to the testimony and autopsy reports of Dr. Stankovic. I checked yesterday to see why I had not received the official motion, and I was informed that the motion had not been filed. Is there a reason for that, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We intended to file. That's why we gave a courtesy copy. We handed over. But due to Registry regulations and policy, it could not be accepted. The motion as such could be accepted, but not the CD that contains about a thousand pages of autopsy reports as an annex to the statement by Dr. Stankovic. And that's why we gave it a follow-up, trying to solve it, because it was not our intention to translate it as it need focus on only a very selective part of it, and we still also are in discussion with the Defence team to what extent we might solve this problem. This means that we will file indeed a motion like this, but please consider it as a draft, because it was goodwill and an intention to file it. But we will get back later to you to update you of the outcome of the discussion with the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I thank you, Mr. Wubben. If there are further -- for the time being, I am not commenting any further. But should you encounter further problems with the Registry with regard to the filing of the annexes to the report, just don't file anything. Come here and I will show you how easy the solution is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So are we ready for the witness? Just before you go, I just want to -- usher, I just want to make sure -- registrar, please -- that he's been spoken to by the victims and witnesses section and that he is fit to give evidence. Have you checked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to the Honourable Trial Chamber, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. And welcome to this Tribunal. Before I proceed any further, but you have already given us an indication, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying in English in a language that you can understand, in your own language, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You'll know the reason for your presence here in this courtroom. You are about to start giving evidence in this case that has been instituted by the Prosecutor against Naser Oric. You're one of the witnesses and you have been summoned to give evidence by the Prosecutor. However, before you start giving evidence, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It's the same words that we use when in some jurisdictions you take an oath before you start to testify. And the legal implications of a solemn declaration are equivalent to those and identical to those of an oath. So, Madam Usher, who is standing next to you, is going to hand to you now the text of the solemn declaration. Please take it your in your hand, read it out loud, and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Radic. You may sit down. Now, let me explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. But before I start, I think it's onerous on my part, a duty on my part as Presiding Judge of this trial, to apologise to you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for having had to bring you twice to The Hague to give evidence. I know, because I am informed, that you were already here in The Hague before the Christmas holidays, but unfortunately, due to the length of time that the previous witness took in concluding his testimony, we could not start with your testimony, and there was no point in starting with your testimony and stopping halfway. So we decided to send you back home and then kindly ask you to return after Christmas, which we did. So I apologise to you for any inconvenience we might have caused to you and to your family, and I thank you for having returned to The Hague to give evidence. The procedure here is going to be as follows: You are first going to be asked a series of questions by Ms. Sellers, who I suppose you have already met, and then she will be followed by Mr. Jones, who is the co-counsel in the team of Defence that is defending, appearing for Mr. Oric. Although you have been produced as a witness, brought forward as a witness by the Prosecutor, in reality, you are no longer now a witness of one side or of the other. You are a witness of the Court. You are a witness of this Tribunal. And your responsibility in terms, in accordance with the oath, with the solemn declaration that you undertook is to answer each and every question that is put to you truthfully and fully as possible, irrespective of who is putting the question. In other words, you have no right to discriminate, say: I will answer fully and truthfully the questions that Ms. Sellers will ask me, but I will not be truthful and fully in my answers when Mr. Jones is putting questions. You have no right to do that. Your responsibility is to be truthful and honest in all your answers to all the questions that are put to you. Did I make myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last thing I want to tell you before we start is that if at any moment, because you will be here for at least today and part of tomorrow for sure, if at any moment you're feeling tired and you need a break, or if you're not feeling well, please draw my attention straight away and we will stop for as long as necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. My name is Judge Agius, Carmel Agius. I come from Malta. To my right I have Judge Brydensholt, who comes from Denmark; to my left, I have Judge Eser, who comes from Germany. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, before addressing the witness, I would ask your permission to lead this witness where it is more likely that we can have a more accelerated and efficient rendering of his testimony. I ask permission for that. But I would like to say also that this witness gives substantial background information, as well as information related to the underlying counts. Some of the background information might appear on its face not to be relevant to some of the specific prison counts, but it is the Prosecution position that background will later cooperate information that other Prosecution witnesses will give. So I would ask your indulgence in some of the areas that might seem more background than actually pertinent for the underlying prison counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take it -- let's have a response from Mr. Jones on the first part, and then we'll tackle the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We would particularly be for the detention charges that we wouldn't want the Prosecution to lead the witness, so obviously for background matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't understand that you were going to lead the witness on those, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I did not intend to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As for the rest, I think we'll have to see how things develop. And I prudently note we haven't -- our attention hasn't been brought to any new areas which might be covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As we'll see, that's more or less our position as well, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll play it by ear as we go along. And obviously if you feel that at any point in time you need to object to a particular question, do rise and object. And then obviously we tackle it. We'll get an explanation. Because I don't know exactly what you are referring to. I will only know when you get there. And if there is an objection. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. I understand, Your Honour. I think it will become apparent and it is no surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I imagine. Okay. Thanks, both of you. We may proceed. You can let the witness on the first part and get going.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic. Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you. My name is Nedeljko Radic. My nickname is Cikota. I was born on the 15th of July, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, would you please confirm for the Trial Chamber that you're a Bosnian Serb and that you were 41 in 1992, precisely, September 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, would you also confirm that in 1992 you lived in the town of Milici, which was in the Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in 1992, you lived with your wife and three children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention very briefly to 1980. Mr. Radic, didn't you begin to work at the state-owned Boksit bauxite mine in Bracan?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And isn't the bauxite mine located in the Vlasenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Furthermore, isn't it correct that the bauxite mine was the second-largest bauxite mine in Europe and a primary source of raw materials to produce aluminum?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, prior to April 1992, could you confirm that the bauxite mine had about 3.000 employees?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Perhaps even more. I'm certain about the 3.000, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And about half of those employees were ethnically Muslims, almost the other half were Serbs, and there was also a small percentage of Romanian employees; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. The percentage was thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then would you please confirm, Mr. Radic, that for 12 years, between 1980 and 1992, you worked as an air compressionist at the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And for the Tribunal -- the Trial Chamber's information, air compressionists at that bauxite mine basically made sure that the equipment at the mine that functioned based upon air pressure, that that machinery was working; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, would you state that the relationship between the Muslims and the Serb workers at the mine was generally good from the time you began to work at the mine in 1980 until the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also, that it was a source of pride in the Vlasenica region to be a worker at the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber what, if anything, happened between the Muslim and the Serb workers at the mine in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Nothing much happened. When the parties were established, the SDA and the SDS, then workers of Muslim -- or rather, Bosniak ethnicity started the leaving the mine en masse. So by the end of May, I think all Bosniaks had left the mine. I'm talking about 1992. Perhaps a handful remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did there also come a time in the spring of 1992, April or May, when one of the buses at the mine was captured?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber the circumstances of that capture.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: A man named Cakura - I don't know his real name - intercepted a bus full of workers at Djile. The bus was full. There were Bosniaks there and Serbs too. Not all of the people in the bus were Serbs. He drove the bus over to Zedanjsko. There's a school building there. The area is actually called Brdo or Brda. That's where the school is. The workers spent the night there, and the next day, following negotiations, I presume they were released. Probably there were party negotiations going on. There was intercession by Mr. Cakura and someone probably negotiated on the part of the Serbs. That's at least what I heard. A man from the SDS, from Pale. I'm not sure where from exactly. So the workers were eventually freed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you testified that there was a man named Cakura. Was he an active member of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was the SDA party a political party that supported the Bosnian Muslim political goals in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a result of the capture of this bus, were the tensions between the Muslim and the Serb workers at the mine escalated in a sense Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that made those relationships worse than before?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, not to that extent. Those who were closer to Cakura had left the mine earlier and the people who were a little more loyal remained at the bauxite mine, to work there. Following this incident, however, it was only to be expected that they too would leave the mine. Only the Serbs remained, and some Romanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did you know this person Cakura before the capture of the bus?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: For about five years. He owned a shop which was in his own house. The distance from the mine was perhaps two or three kilometres. We would go to his shop practically on a daily basis, to buy cigarettes or whatever else we needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to this Cakura personally, then?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him speak, meaning were you familiar with his voice if he spoke to other persons?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the voice. I think I could still recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as a result of many of the Muslim employees leaving the mine, did the mine cease to function?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. The mine continued to operate, but with less capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, in May 1992, during this period of employees leaving the mine, did your job function modify? Did you take on other duties at the mine?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: We received a different roster. For this reason, some of the workers had to secure the mine. I was among those workers. We were guards there, sort of. We stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber, then: As a guard, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The same as before the war, the guards before the war. Every company in the former Yugoslavia had those. I'm not sure about the rest of the world. Every company had guards who stood guard and watched over the equipment. There were workshops there, machines, kitchens, and the management, at least in the main branch of a certain company. So that's what they watched and that was their task.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a guard, were you issued a rifle or another form of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: A rifle. The rifles, before the war, every Territorial Defence unit, national Territorial Defence unit, had these rifles. So the TO had weapons. Those were M-48 rifles, for the most part, and we would sign for those rifles, those of us who secured the mine, the guards, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were those rifles, were they your own personal weapons or were they weapons that belonged to the company?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. The company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you worked as a guard, these additional duties at the mine, were you considered a soldier or were you considered a civilian mine worker?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was a worker, a miner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, now I want to turn your attention to the summer of 1992, between June and September. Were there trucks, buses, or other transport owned by the mine, were these vehicles ever involved in ambushes?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber the nature of the ambushes that these transport vehicles were subjected to.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Those were village ambushes, mostly the trucks that were carrying or were stopped occasionally at the so-called checkpoints or barricades, at a place called Djile, or Zutica, Konjevic Polje. In those three locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber who or what group were stopping the transport vehicles.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. Cakura was probably aware of who was doing it in Djile, and I don't know about the other two locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether these were Muslims or whether they were Serbs who were stopping the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I think it was Muslims, because those places had 100 Muslim population. Or rather, Djile and Zutica had 100 Muslim population, and even in Konjevic Polje, there were about 80 per cent of Muslims, although there were some Serb family houses as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a result of these vehicles being stopped, were any of the drivers or persons on those vehicles killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many drivers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you became a guard at the mine. Who were you guarding the mine from?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: From Muslims, because the war had already begun and we all got our wartime assignments. Although we were not guarding only from Muslims; we were guarding it from anyone. We were there to protect the mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did there come a time when the mine was attacked?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 24th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber what you were doing on the morning of the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: That morning, around 9.00 a.m., I had breakfast and then we set out to get some water, five of us guards. We took a piece of mining equipment, a loader, which we had used before to get water. When we set out, we took two rifles, as usual, two M-48 rifles, and we went down to a place called Bracan, to Bozo's house. And I stood on the bonnet of this loader, and I was standing there when they started shooting at us, at the machine perhaps, not at me personally. And then we abandoned the idea of going to get water. We abandoned the machine and decided to go back to Bracan, where we had set out from. However, two of my fellow workers remained by Bozo's house, namely, Slavko and Krnja, K-r-n-j-a. Whereas three of us went back to Bracan: myself, Nedeljko Radic; and Zoran Lalovic; and Vidoje Salipurevic. When we were already close to Bracan -- it is an elevation, so that when the road was dug out, the barrier was about two metres high, and on that side next to the boundary, next to the barrier, was I, and next to me were Vidoje Salipurevic and Zoran Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, thank you. I would just like to ask you a couple of questions about what you have just testified about. The vehicle that you were in, was it a vehicle that belonged to the mining company?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was used for loading ore.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. It was not a military vehicle, was it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that at a point there was shooting and you stopped, you got out of the vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you from where the vehicle stopping, could you see the town of Podravanje, or the village of Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there anything in particular that appeared to be happening at the village of Podravanje that morning, the 24th of September?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was burning. Smoke was coming up in clouds, columns.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you returned, when you left the vehicle and you started to return back to Bracan, where the mine was, did you have any weapons with you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: There were those two rifles, and I don't know if you gentlemen and ladies are aware of it. Those are M-48 rifles, which can take five rounds, plus one in the barrel. Two rifles of that kind remained with Slavko and Krnja at that house, because they had carried the rifles in the first place. Of course, they returned gunfire and ran out of ammunition, and we didn't need the empty rifles any more, because we were going to Bracan, and our rifles were up there in Bracan, in a small cottage normally used for camping, where we spent our nights. And we never Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond reached them, because of what happened. Zoran and Vidoje were killed and I was captured, without any weapon, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to the mine, to Bracan, would you please describe what you saw happening at the mine upon your arrival.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: When I was captured, I was personally captured by Zulfo Tursunovic, whom I had known before. I also knew his brother and Milehu [phoen] and many other people. There were many other co-workers who used to work with him at the mine, Muslim workers, who on that occasion beat me up and tied me down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, when you say they beat you up and tied you down, how did they beat you? And would you please tell the Trial Chamber whether at that point this person you describe as Zulfo was present.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. They tied my hands behind my back, and a couple of minutes later -- my nickname was Cikota, and a relative of mine had been in prison together with Zulfo before the war. And it is most likely that it was he who saved me then. So then Zulfo ordered three men, whom I didn't know, including a person named or referred to as Beli, as far as I can remember, ordered them to take me to Zulfo's house, in a place called Vijogor, where they were supposed to await further orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Before he issued that order to take me away, he took some kind of notepad, and as five of my co-workers were lying dead around me, I was supposed to give him their names, and he took them down in this notepad. And the five men were -- shall I tell you the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Those were Slavko Salipurevic, Vidoje Salipurevic, Zoran Lalovic, Rajko Antic, and Miso Misic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'd like to ask you: When you went back to the mine and you said that you had your hands tied, people were kicking you, could you tell me whether the people who were tying your hands or kicking you, were they wearing -- what type of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: There were many in civilian clothing. Some wore uniforms, including Zulfo, who had a camouflage uniform on. At that time, I didn't even know what an American camouflage uniform looked like, until I was told. And there were many people carrying weapons, hunting rifles, shotguns, which said to me that they were not active-duty army troops. Those were local people, most of whom I knew, people from Djile, Zedanjsko, Tuzeri, Zutica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you also tell me whether Zulfo Tursunovic was carrying a weapon.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What type of weapon was he carrying?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: An automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did he at any time participate in the beating of you while you were tied and on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: He was there. He was probably watching. I was kicked down to the ground and I wasn't able to look around any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic had been in gaol before. Do you know why he had been in gaol before?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had killed two persons in Srebrenica, in a barroom owned by a Serb. The two men whom Zulfo had killed were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you describe Zulfo Tursunovic physically for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: He was probably 1.7 metres tall, with a pudgy, reddish face, stocky, looking rather strong. I don't know what he looks like now. I haven't seen him since.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you approximately know what age he had at that period, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: He could have been 60, perhaps, but he didn't look more than 50. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zulfo Tursunovic is Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the other people who were at that mine that day that you described as wearing uniforms, do you know whether they were Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Of course they were Muslims. I don't know. Maybe there was a Serb among them as well, but I rather doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I have to ask you the same question: In terms of the civilians that were with the Muslim soldiers that day, the people in uniform, do you know whether they were Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, is it your testimony that it was Zulfo Tursunovic who appeared to be giving orders that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did he appear to be giving orders to the uniformed men who were at the mine?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I think he gave orders to everybody, civilians and those in uniform alike.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did you see anybody giving orders to Zulfo Tursunovic that day at the mine?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did Zulfo Tursunovic have in his possession or on him that day a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what is a Motorola, or the type of Motorola that Zulfo Tursunovic had on him that day.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It's not unlike a mobile telephone, although it's longer, with an extended aerial, the sort of equipment that the police have usually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that it was Zulfo Tursunovic who took you around to your dead former colleagues and asked you what their names were. Did Zulfo Tursunovic look surprised at all that those men at the mine were dead?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was it your impression that day that your colleagues had been killed by either the soldiers or the civilians that were present at the mine that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All of them were together, the civilians and those men in uniform, and it's most likely that they were under the command of Zulfo Tursunovic, at least. That's what I firmly believe, but I wasn't there. I couldn't tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that Zulfo Tursunovic gave an order to have you removed from the mine. Would you tell the Trial Chamber under what circumstances did you then leave the mine that morning, after Zulfo gave the order?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... testimony that Zulfo Tursunovic gave an order to have him removed from the mine. I really don't recall him saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Why don't -- Your Honour, I believe that he did say that earlier, but I will certainly -- can rephrase the question and ask:

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did Zulfo Tursunovic give any order in regard to you leaving the mine that morning?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the time being. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radic. I believe you just answered. I asked whether Zulfo Tursunovic gave an order to have you removed from the mine. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber -- and I believe the witness answered yes to the question. Would you then tell the Trial Chamber how you left the mine, with whom did you leave the mine, what were the circumstances of you leaving the mine at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: My hands were tied behind my back. I was escorted by three men, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond one of them in uniform, two of them in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The person who was in uniform, did you know or did you come to know his name?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The two people who were civilians, did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: One was called Beli, and I didn't know about the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as you left the mine, did you pass the house of Bozo, that you had described or testified earlier as the house where your two fellow guards went to?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell me, tell the Trial Chamber, did you see those two guards again who had sought refuge in Bozo's house?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Those men who had been killed were there in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are those men Slavko Gordic and Krnja?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As you were now walking with your armed escorts, did any other prisoners or people under arrest join you in your walk?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kukic and Nevenko joined me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were they walking by themselves or were they walking with other people?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They were walking together with me, with their hands tied as well, and we went up to Zulfo's house, where those armed escorts awaited further orders to transport us to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how many armed escorts were with you, Kukic, and Nevenko?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The same three that had set out with me from Bracan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as you were walking towards Zulfo Tursunovic's house, did any of those persons walking with you have a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you were walking in the house -- towards Zulfo Tursunovic's house, did any of those persons, those armed persons walking with you, hit you or strike you with any instruments or with their hands or feet?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They beat us in the village of Kutezero [phoen], when we arrived there, they were joined by another man, and that's where we were beaten. That newly arrived man had some portable radio which he used to transmit to somebody words to the effect that the operation is going on successfully. That's all I was able to hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know what operation he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I ask one moment? Could I ask the usher to please move the ELMO back a bit. I think there's a slight line of sight that's a bit perturbing. Yes. Could you just remove that. I'm seeing that -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, about how long did it take you to get to Zulfo Tursunovic's house that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: About two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Zulfo Tursunovic's house, did you see people dressed in uniforms near and around his house?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: There were people around his house. I didn't go inside. Most of those around the house were civilians, although there were two uniformed men as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay outside of Zulfo Tursunovic's house that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: An hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you still under armed escort at that point or had your hands been untied and were you allowed to move around freely?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. The armed escorts did not change. Our hands remained tied.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you described two people having joined you, one called Kukic and another called Nevenko. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you knew Mr. Nevenko prior to seeing him that day as you walked to Zulfo Tursunovic's house.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: This Nevenko and Kukic were men whom I had come to know two or three months prior. They are originally from Indjija, in Serbia. They were hired by the mine, under a three-month contract or something, to work in the security detail, as guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Radic, it's your testimony that both Mr. Kukic and Nevenko were also employees at the mine?, the bauxite mine, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, while you were waiting at the house of Zulfo Tursunovic, did there come a time period when you and the other two men were removed to another place?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me rephrase that. Did there come a time when you were placed in a truck and removed from the area of Zulfo Tursunovic's house?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell me how you and the other men were placed in the truck and describe for Your Honours your positions.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was a small truck. When they put us on the truck, we were all three of us seated, with our hands tied, of course, and there were another three men with us. Two of them were armed and one wasn't. There were all three of them in civilian clothing. This man called Beli was seated. I think he was an ethnic Albanian, or at least that's what I found out at a later date. He used to work at the Srebrenica Sase mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, who was driving the truck?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the people who were in the truck with you in the back other than Beli?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers in the truck?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether you were being removed as a result of an order of Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Most probably. When he said that they were to await orders at his house, so that was the assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the truck and the truck, I presume, was moving, did anything happen to you, Mr. Kukic, or Nevenko?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They took Kukic's watch off, my shoes and trousers. It was civilian clothing, of course. It was autumn time, and the shoes were made for winter. That was probably the reason they liked them. They hit us here and there. They made threats, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, where did this truck eventually take you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: To Srebrenica, outside the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, is that the town of Srebrenica or are you just referring generally to the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you go to the town of Srebrenica, in Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. The police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And around what time of the day was it now when you arrived at the SUP in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was night already. I can't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you still under armed guard when you arrived at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, upon arrival, would you tell the Trial Chamber where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Inside the SUP building, to a room that was three or four square metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did this room have bars on it or was it an open, normal room?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber how many people were placed into that room with bars on it at that time.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The three of us came first: Kukic, Nevenko, and myself. During the night, Veselin Sarac and Zoran Bankovic joined us. There were five of us at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you know Veselin Sarac and Zoran Bankovic before you were placed in a cell with them in September 1992? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I did know Veselin. He worked at the bauxite mine. And I did not know Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were Muslims or whether they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had been arrested by Muslim soldiers or by civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know where they had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: In Podravanje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is Podravanje the village that you testified earlier that had been burning when your loader was stopped and you saw from the hillside?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the cell was, I believe, three by four metres. Could you please indicate for the Trial Chamber whether the cell had any windows in it, whether the cell had any beds in it, and whether the cell had any toilet facilities in it.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I didn't say it was three by four. I said it was three or four square metres. The size, three by four, that means twelve square metres, which is a rather large space.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My apologies. Would you please correct me and indicate for the Trial Chamber, then, the correct dimensions of the cell.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Three or four square metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Maybe one and a half by two metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any beds in the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any chairs in the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there toilet facilities in the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there open windows or air ventilation places in the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: There was some sort of a window, an opening, but it was not a proper window. There was no glass pane. It was just empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: From your point of view was there room enough in the cell forever any of the men, Bankovic, Kukic, Nevenko, yourself, to be able to lie down comfortably in the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Not really lying down properly. There were two square metres of floor down there, and the rest was just a concrete slab. So it was too cold.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, on that first night, the 24th of September, 1992, did anything happen to you or the other men who were in the cell with you in terms of physical mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The next day after we were captured, we were taken out for an interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I just have you answer the question. That first night that you were there, did anything happen to you in terms of physical mistreatment, the night that you arrived?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. No, not when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now could you tell the Trial Chamber, yes, on the second day that you were there, you were testifying that you were taken out for interrogation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: To a police chief. I'm not sure what his name was. He wore a beard. I was brought to see him. We were taken out one by one. Of course, there was another civilian sitting there, and the chief too was in plain clothes. He asked me whether I smoked. I said yes. He gave me a cigarette, tobacco. I took it. And he started to kick me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, you said that you were taken out. Does that mean that you were taken out of the cell that you've just described for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were you taken to another --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: To another room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And do you know where this other room was in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you describe how you got from your cell to the other room, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: There's a corridor. Once I was out of the room, I headed straight for a door down the corridor. That room was larger, and that's where the two people were. Therefore, first I left the cell. To the left, there was one room; to the right, there was a flight of stairs leading up to the first floor, and another down to the cellar. I headed straight down the corridor and the chief's room was at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did you leave your cell on your own? Did you just open up the cell door or the door with the bars on it and go to the room, or did someone take you there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know who it was. A guard, perhaps, or the person who kept the keys to the cell and the prison. There were two persons in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you said that when you were in the room being interrogated, that you think it might have been a chief of police. Could you please describe what that person was wearing.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can remember. He had some sort of a T-shirt, a pair of trousers, a long beard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was he wearing --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: That's at least as far as I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Was he -- were any of the other persons in the room wearing uniforms or what appeared to be military clothing?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. No. Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were you treated during that interrogation as a prisoner of war, meaning were you asked your name, your rank, your serial number, any military affiliation?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to know my name, whether I was a soldier, and what my rank was, who my commander was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did they tell you whether you had been charged with any crime or illegal activity?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. It's difficult for me to say how they treated me. I know they asked me about my rank and my commander. Of course, I told them that I had no rank, that I was not a soldier, that I was a worker. Every time I replied, I would be hit by this chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, where would this chief hit you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was seated on a chair. He would kick me in the chest, over my face.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can you recall about how many times that you were kicked or hit during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: About three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a result of being kicked or hit, did you suffer pain? Were you bleeding? Were there any bruises forming on your body?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any injuries, but it did hurt, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you then taken back to your cell after the interrogation or were you taken to another place in the building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you went back to your cell, do you recall whether you were bleeding or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, you do not recall, or no, you were not bleeding?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was not bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you returned to the cell, was anyone else of the men who were with you in the cell then taken out for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took Veselin Sarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did Veselin Sarac come back to the cell after he had been interrogated?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he also was physically mistreated, such as beaten, when he went for his interrogation that morning? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't present. But he said that he had a tougher time than I did, because he was bleeding when he came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know that if after Veselin Sarac was Mr. Kukic or Zoran Bankovic or Nevenko, were they also called out to be interrogated that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were they interrogated on other days that you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Staying on the 25th of September, 1992: Would you tell the Trial Chamber what happened, if anything, that evening.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: That evening, a man came to the cell. At night, there was no electricity, no lighting. And they took us out one by one. Veselin Sarac was the first to be taken out. I don't know what they did to him in that room. That was another room that was across the way from the cell. After a while, he was returned. Then they took me out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, when you say that "they" took Veselin Sarac out and then "they" took you out --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: From the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: From the cell. Would you please describe, to the best of your ability, what the people, they, looked like who took you out of the cell.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They wore [Realtime transcript read in error "swore"] civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And where did they take you to? Another room in the SUP building, you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The same building, the adjacent room. They kept taking us there to beat us. There was some sort of a reception room that's next to the street entrance. Kemo from Pale was there in that room almost every evening. Whenever they took us out, we would find Kemo there. And a man they called Mrki was usually with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's just a matter with the transcript. As we understand, the witness when asked, and it's line 24, page 31, he said they were civilians as opposed to they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, it's "they swore," "they swore."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's to the effect that I think he just said "civilians," I don't think he mentioned clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean I wouldn't be able to tell you that. Mr. Radic, you were asked earlier on, from the cell, would you please describe for the best of your ability, what the people, they looked like when -- who took you out of the cell. Did -- what was your answer? You described what they were wearing or did you say they were just civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That evening, civilian, civilian clothes. When I say "civilian," that means the person is wearing civilian clothes, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it and proceed, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the people who were wearing civilian clothes were they carrying weapons or could you see whether they were armed or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You testified that these people then took you to another room where there was a Kemo, someone called Kemo, and windows. Is this a room in the SUP building where there is a stove?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I apologise. I will correct your question a little. Those were not just persons. There was a person wearing civilian clothes who took us out. I found out later that his name was Cude and he was wearing civilian clothes. He would take us to that very room. And that's where they beat us and mistreated us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the name Kemo, and you said that they would beat us. Is Kemo a nickname or is that someone's full name?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I found out later his real name, Kemal Ahmetovic. I don't know whether it's true, but the way people referred to him at the time was Kemo from Pale. Probably the reference was to a place called Pale, or maybe it was just another nickname. I really can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Trial Chamber how Kemo was dressed. What clothing was he wearing, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you also describe what Kemo looked like physically.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: He was a very strong man, young, 170 centimetres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any other men in that room with the stove who were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: This man they called Mrki was wearing civilian clothes, and there were two other men wearing civilian clothes, or suits, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did this man Mrki, could you describe what he looked like physically.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Very tall, over two metres. A big, burly man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you did testify that going to that room is where you would receive a beating. Would you tell the Trial Chamber, on that first day that you went to the room, what type of beating you yourself received.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was beaten. They used their fists and they kicked me too. I'm talking about that evening. I'm not sure how I should put it. There were logs stacked up there. There was an oven. And there were logs stacked there a metre high.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did they use the logs to beat you with?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was for firewood, but they used it every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did Kemo beat you that night?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How would he beat you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: First he kicked me. Then he used his fists. And then Mrki also hit me several times. They kept me there for a while. They went to get Kukic. Not they, but the guard, rather, the man called Cude. He brought Kukic over and they started beating him then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They started insulting him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just want to mention, we'll return to the beating of Mr. Kukic later on. Was Veselin Sarac beaten that night or Zoran Bankovic or Nevenko?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: We were all beaten. I said that Sarac was the first to be taken out, and then he was returned to the cell, and then they came for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Sarac returned to the cell, could you describe how he looked when he came back to the cell as opposed to how he looked when he had left the cell that day, or that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was night. It was very difficult for me to see anything. It was dark. I really can't tell you what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you see him the following morning?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did he have the appearance of someone who had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what did that look like to you, Mr. Radic, the fact that he had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't really pay that much attention to Veselin. I tried to look after myself, because I hurt very badly. They cracked me over the back and over the chest with the log. I had fractures. This proved to be the case later, after I was exchanged. I was suffering severe pain and some of my teeth were smashed. Therefore, I wasn't paying much attention to the state that Veselin Sarac was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to ask possibly could we break at this time period because then I'll be moving into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact I was going to draw your attention, Ms. Sellers, that you only had two or three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I think rather than continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll break for 25 minutes. Would that be enough for you, Mr. Radic, or do you require more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite enough. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and then we resume soon after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sellers. Do you think you will finish with the witness today?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: There is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I see it, there is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm gauging it --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I myself am noticing it too. There might be just a little bit of overlap tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. In which case, you would be able to finish in one sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Thank you. Let's proceed, Ms. Sellers, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you were testifying that you had been taken to the room where there was a stove and the pieces of wood, and you were beaten. My question now is: You have described someone named Mrki as wearing civilian clothes. Do you ever recall, when you said that that person might have been wearing a uniform or military clothes while he was in that room and administering beatings?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did you speak to investigators from the Office of the Prosecution in May, in the year 2000? More specifically, a female investigator named Eileen Gilleece? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you also recall that she took a statement that basically recounted your experiences at the SUP building, and that after the statement was taken, that you read the statement over and that you signed her name to the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission, I would like to read out two sections of that statement and ask the witness if he remember having given that as his prior statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I will ask you whether you recall having stated or having told the investigator that "he was dressed" and the "he" at this point - I am not trying to be confusing - does not refer to Mrki but to another person. It says: "He was dressed in a yellow khaki beige uniform, which is called an American uniform. On the left breast pocket of his shirt he wore a patch that had lilies on it. It was a special uniform. Only he and Mrki wore uniforms like that. Later I met another commander named Mrki." And then do you recall having told the investigator that, in relationship to the uniform of a person called Mrki?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mrki? No. Unless there are two persons called Mrki. The description is all right with the lilies. But that was the sort of uniform that Kemo wore.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And might I now read out another paragraph from that statement. This is in reference to the room with the wood-burning stove: "Two other soldiers were in the room. One was dressed in an American uniform, a special one, like the one Naser Oric wore. It was the same colour and type, and he wore the same patch with lilies on the left breast. Kemo called this soldier Mrki. Mrki did not have a pistol on him at that time." Do you recall telling the investigator from the Office of the Prosecution that information in your statement in May of 2000?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't remember about the uniform. Again, I'm saying only there were two persons called Mrki. I only knew of one myself. That's all I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question that is being asked with you is not whether you remember now about the uniforms, but whether what has been read out to you by Ms. Sellers are your actual words to the investigators when you gave the statement way back in -- I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: May 2000, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about the uniform, that much is certain. I did give that statement, but I don't remember about Mrki and the uniform specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you described the beating that you received when you were in the room with the wood-burning stove. During that beating, did you lose any of the teeth that were in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber how you came to lose your teeth during that time.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Kemo was beating me, as well as Mrki, the Mrki that I know. He was a civilian. They punched me, kicked me, breaking my teeth. All that happened that evening. It was the second night, the first night after I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did they use any instruments to remove your teeth or did they remove your -- did your teeth fall out as a result of blows or kicks?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Not that night. The next night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please describe to the Trial Chamber what happened to you in relationship to your teeth on the following evening.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The next day and the next evening, because nobody maltreated us or beat us by day, only at night, except when we went to the lavatory, if somebody happened to be in the hallway, they would hit us in passing. Once I was hit in passing with an iron bar. They would also kick us, punch us. So that next night when I was taken out, Kemo started to beat me again, and then he took pliers and extracted the bits of teeth that were left after the beating of the previous night, the teeth that were already broken. The pliers were very broad, so he could get two or three teeth in the same go. And after that, he disinfected the wound with urine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, when you had your teeth extracted by Kemo, were you given any type of medication or sedative in order to diminish the pain of the extraction of the teeth?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. No. There was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you say that then your teeth or your mouth were disinfected by urine, would it be your testimony that Kemo or another person put urine in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kemo did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber where were you in the SUP building when your teeth were extracted and when Kemo urinated in your mouth.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It's the room with the wood-burning stove.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you have described having been beaten on your first full day, the 25th [Realtime transcript read in error "20th"] of September, by Mr. Kemo, and there were other people present, such as Mrki, and this happened again on the 26th of September, 1992, when your teeth were extracted. Were there other times during your stay in the prison when you were taken to the room with the wooden stove and beaten or maltreated?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, every time they took us out and brought us there, they would beat us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would that happen every day within a 24-hour period during your stay at the prison?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, to separate day from night, I have to say that nobody touched us by day. We were left alone. And we were not even beaten every night, because when Cude was the turnkey, so to say, of that prison, he Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond wouldn't allow anyone to do any harm to us, and we were safe from harm every time he was the duty guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, Judge Eser is drawing my attention that perhaps the date of the 26th of September is wrong. Is it the 26th or the 25th? 20th. Sorry, not the 26th. The 20th is wrong. On line 14. You asked the witness: "So you've described having been beaten on your first full day, the 20th of September."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I meant to say the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 25th. Okay. So that goes for the record. You can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you stated that you were principally beaten in the evening hours, and particularly when there was a guard Cude who was not present. When there were other guards, were the beatings more frequent and more assured that they would take place?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the guards changed every day. They took turns. I singled out one of them. He was a policeman, because he wore a police uniform. He would come to our cell and he wouldn't even let us go to the lavatory. So I drew the conclusion that he was also one of the turnkeys. I don't know the name of this policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would there be a pattern that you would be taken out of the cell and always taken to this room in the evening, and there you would be beaten?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you sometimes beaten more than once or twice in the same evening?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they would barge into the cell, one or two of them, beat us inside the cell, and then take us out into that room, where they would continue beating us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the people who beat you, did that usually include Kemo and Mrki and other people that you've described for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Nine times out of ten, Kemo and Mrki were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there also people who came from outside of the SUP building? Were they allowed in and permitted to beat you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did you see, while you were in the room with the wooden stove, did you see any of the other prisoners who were with you, Zoran Bankovic, Nevenko, Veselin Sarac? Did you also see them being beaten?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you describe to the Trial Chamber the manner in which that they were beaten. Were they kicked, hit, were instruments used, were there wooden logs used? Please describe what you saw to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Everybody got the same treatment, the same beatings, kicking, punching. That was the usual method. I was the only one, together with Kukic, who was killed the second night, on whom wooden logs were used. In the same room. I was there when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask you: Would you remind the Trial Chamber what day, or 24-hour period, I mean, was it in which you say that Kukic was killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I think the next day, in the evening, after we were captured, and I'm pretty sure that is right because he was killed the same evening my teeth were extracted by Kemo. I think it was the second night, yes, because we were left alone the first night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So would it be your testimony, then, that Mr. Kukic was killed on the 25th of September. That would be the night that your teeth had been knocked out due to beating.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know who killed Mr. Kukic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I know because I was there when Kemo was doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what Kemo was doing exactly that resulted in the death of Mr. Kukic.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: That happened. We were in Sarac's office when he was returned to his cell, and I was the next one to be taken out. I was beaten there, and after a couple of minutes, they brought Kukic, and then they started beating him. Mrki felled him to the ground, cursing at the same time, mentioning, I believe, his Ustasha mother. Then Kemo took this piece of wood, and as Kemo was lying on his back, he hit him on the chest, and he was dead on the spot. There was a bottle of water sitting on the windowsill, and Kemo poured it into his mouth, but it was too late. And then he ordered me to haul him back to the cell. So I bent down to lift the body. I couldn't manage, because I was hurting all over from the beating. And then Kemo took that same piece of wood and hit me on the back again, so that I fell right on top of Kukic. Then they hoisted me up, threw me into the cell, and afterwards, Zoran and Slavenko went out and brought Kukic's dead body back into the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When Mr. Kukic was being beaten, about how close were you to Mr. Kukic and to Kemo?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It's one metre's distance. It's in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you had been beaten, and can you just confirm to the Trial Chamber that you were beaten before Mr. Kukic was brought into the room.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was taken out before Kukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would it be your testimony that even though you had been beaten by Kemo prior to you witnessing the beating that killed Kukic, that you were able to clearly see Kemo and Mrki beating Mr. Kukic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you said that in the beating of Mr. Kukic, that they used pieces of wood. Would you show the Trial Chamber more or less how long and how broad the pieces of wood that they were using were.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, they were rather long, maybe 80 centimetres, maybe 1 metre, short enough to be -- to fit into the stove.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you yourself had been hit previously by Kemo, Mrki, using these pieces of wood. My question to you is: Did the blows that you received inflict pain upon your body when they used the wood?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
