utterances.text: Did you see them hit Mr. Kukic using what could be tantamount to the same type of force that they used when they hit you with the blocks of wood?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Kemo was the only one who was hitting him, not Mrki, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was Kemo using the same type of force that was used against you with the blocks of wood?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Even greater force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was the cursing, the calling of Mr. Kukic "Ustasha," was this occurring at the same time that they were administering these powerful blows with the wood, their hands, or their feet?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Sorry. They didn't call Kukic Ustasha. On the contrary; Kukic was cursing the Ustasha mothers of Mrki and the other man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My apologies. That's correct. And do you think that while he was cursing them, that's when the blows were being administered to him? Is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I saw. Then Kemo took this split log, probably angry at being cursed, and he hit him so hard that he killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So is it your opinion that Kukic died immediately after this blow that Kemo administered?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It took a couple of seconds, because I saw it. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You've testified that the now body of Mr. Kukic was taken back to the cell. Did the body remain in the cell with you and now the four remaining prisoners that evening?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. It remained there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The other prisoners who were in the room now - Mr. Nevenko, Zoran Bankovic and Veselin Sarac - had they been beaten that evening also?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were they also beaten in the room with the wooden stove? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were they beaten by Kemo and by Mrki and whoever else had been in the room?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there with them. I don't know who beat them. It's most probable that Kemo was present, judging by their stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the following morning, did Kemo come to the cell where the body of Kukic was laying?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did he inquire about Kukic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. He asked what had happened to him, as if he didn't know. And I believe some of -- one of us answered that it was a heart attack, although we all knew perfectly well what had happened. However, fearing for our own lives, we did not want to say what actually happened, thinking that maybe the next evening the same might happen to us. We didn't want to say that Kemo had killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Kukic showed no signs of life after he left the room with the wooden stove and no signs of life throughout the rest of that night while he was in your cell. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the body of Mr. Kukic removed from the cell sometime during that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber who removed the body of Mr. Kukic from the cell.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Kemo came. It could have been around 10.00 a.m. I could be off by 30 minutes. Anyway, he ordered us to take Kukic's body out. We lifted the body. The truck was parked outside the SUP building. A yellow, big truck, FAP-type. So we put the body on the truck and were escorted back to our cell. Then Kemo came again and took Veselin Sarac away. We didn't know where. All we knew was that he didn't come back for another two hours, and he left on the same truck that took Kukic's body away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you testified that "we took the body out," that means that you assisted in the removal of Mr. Kukic's body. Who else was with you taking the body out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zoran, myself, and Sarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you placed the body on the truck, was there a guard or someone who was escorting you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was Kemo present when you placed the body on the truck?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you returned to your cell, Kemo came back to take out Veselin Sarac. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber: Where was Veselin Sarac from originally?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. What do you mean by where was he from?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where did he live?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The village of Podravanje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When Veselin Sarac came back to the cell after two hours, after having left with the body of Kukic, did he tell you where Mr. Kukic's body was taken?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber what Mr. Sarac told you about the disposal of Mr. Kukic's body.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was taken to Podravanje, his home village, where the bauxite ore was mined. A large pit remained from the mining, and it is now filled with water. It is a water reservoir now. And it was already a reservoir then. And when they reached the reservoir -- I forgot to mention that Sarac was tied to those bars in the truck, probably to prevent escape. And when the body was thrown, literally thrown, not taken out of the truck, onto the ground, near the reservoir, Kemo shot at Kukic, so that the Chetnik wouldn't rise. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, has the body of Mr. Kukic ever been recovered and given a proper burial?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. I was home recently. Some team arrived, including his family, to search the reservoir, and they searched and searched, but they didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, in your conversation with Veselin Sarac about being on the truck and the disposal of Mr. Kukic's body, did he say whether there was anyone else other than Kemo who was present in the truck?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were another two men. The driver, plus another person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the other persons were soldiers or wearing military garb?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I would like to resume and ask you a couple of questions about your imprisonment at the SUP. After the death of Mr. Kukic, did any other -- were any other prisoners placed in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did you remain in the cell with Zoran Bankovic, Veselin Sarac, Nevenko?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did the beatings, as you testified before, continue on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, except when Cude was around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: About ten days into your imprisonment, did another prisoner arrive at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this other prisoner?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I know they called him the postman. He was from Fakovici. But I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you remember more or less how old this person you refer to as the postman was, at that time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I think quite old, might have been around 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you remember or could you describe for the Trial Chamber whether he was a tall person, a small person, whether he was a large person?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. He was small, small.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether, while he was imprisoned at the SUP with you in that cell, do you know whether he was taken out and beaten, as the other prisoners that you described were beaten?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was he beaten on a regular basis, similar to yourself and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The same applied to everyone, more or less. Now, who was beaten more, I can't say. I know about myself, how many times I was beaten, and how. I don't know about the rest. We would be taken out one by one, so I wasn't present when the other people were being beaten. Therefore, I can't say how long they were beaten for and in what way exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During the day, were you able to see what the other prisoners in your cell looked like, what their physical appearance would be?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Of course, they were black and blue and very tired, exhausted. Nevenko could not even stand up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did any of those prisoners, due to these beatings, also have their teeth knocked out?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I only know about myself, but I think this was the case with Veselin Sarac also. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of those prisoners would then have bruises on their face or on other parts of their body?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: On the face, yes. Veselin Sarac and Nevenko too, myself included, with my teeth having been smashed or extracted. I had injuries on my gums too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that when you came to the SUP building, that some of your clothing had been removed during the truck ride. Would you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond please tell the Trial Chamber what clothes you were wearing during that period of your imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: While I was in the cell, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I was only wearing my shorts. That was all. Cude brought me a blanket, a small pillow. So I used that to keep warm, and that's how I remained. That blanket was the only thing I had until I was eventually exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did you see your fellow inmates now progressively becoming physically weaker during your stay and looking physically worse during your stay in the prison?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Of course. Zoran was a little younger. He was 18 at the time. He was a little more resistant than the rest of us, probably. And the rest of us, Veselin and Nevenko, were in a very poor state. I think I was coping a little better than they were. At least I was able to stand up. But my brain was practically numb. I couldn't remember anything. I couldn't even think straight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you were able to stand up. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what the other inmates were able to do, given their physical condition in terms of positioning themselves within this cell.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They would just sit down and lean against the wall, like that, the whole time. Sometimes, if they were able, they would try to stand up for a while, and then they would sit down again. There was no room to lie down. There was too little space for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You testified earlier about being beat as you were on your way to the toilets.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you went to the toilet, do you know who it was who was beating you, what type of people?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Mostly there would be people in civilian clothing there, two or three persons. My conclusion was that they were most probably locals. Whenever they took any one of us out of the cell to take us to the lavatory, they were just there in the corridor and they would start beating us with whatever was at hand. Nevenko was probably beaten more outside in the corridor, because he was the one who asked to go to the lavatory the most. He was probably beaten more outside in the corridor than inside the room in which we were being kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a result of these beatings on the way to the lavatory, did you attempt or did you try to go to the lavatory as less frequently as possible?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case with me. I would not ask to go to the lavatory for two or three days at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, where was the lavatory located in the SUP building, the one that you've described?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The lavatory was contiguous to the cell. Once outside in the hallway, it was the first door on the left, next to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you ever asked to clean the lavatory?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what did cleaning the lavatory entail?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: There was no running water to flush the toilet. Therefore, Sarac and Veselin in particular were forced to gather it up with their bare hands. I only had to do it once, because I didn't go to the lavatory that often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: After cleaning the toilets out with their bare hands, were they able to wash their hands?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. They would just wipe them on their own clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. I would now like to ask you some other questions concerning your stay at the SUP prison. Did there come a time period when someone, to your knowledge, named Naser Oric, came to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but, Your Honour, I made it very clear at the outset that when it came to the detention charges, that if we really insist that the Prosecution not ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This witness knows this is the trial of Naser Oric. She knows perfectly well how to ask a question, "Did there come a time when a person came to the cell." She is providing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken, Mr. Jones, and I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I will rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's the case of rephrasing it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did there come a time period when someone came to the cell and introduced themselves as --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question should be did a person ever come --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think counsel does not have to ask a question for me, particularly one that I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let her finish the question, please, Mr. Jones. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My question would have been: Would there -- would there come a time when someone came to the cell and presented themselves as someone who was in charge of the SUP or the prison or who had some type of power within that building?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object to that question. It's completely leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what grounds now? It's a perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question should really be: Did anyone else ever come to the cell, did they ever say anything, what did they say. There are perfectly proper non-leading questions which can be put to elicit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is also perfectly entitled to ask whether at any time anyone who appeared to be in command or a person in authority ever visited the cell or the building, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is a way of getting evidence with a completely leading question, whereas there's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a leading question. I mean it's distinguishing one person or one type of person from another. Yes, Ms. Sellers. I think it's the case of trying to combine what Mr. Jones has suggested and your question which I still consider to be perfectly legitimate. But I think it's the case also of putting the question again, because in the meantime there has been a lapse of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did anyone, Mr. Radic, come to your cell and introduce themselves as someone who had power or was in charge of the prison?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, no one really introduced themselves. But Mr. Naser used to come. He would only introduce himself, saying: My name is Naser Oric, in case you didn't know. But he never really introduced himself as being commander. He would come in uniform, with the lilies, camouflage uniform, but he did not introduce himself, saying that he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did other prisoners or did anyone else who was in the SUP building ever tell you that Naser Oric was the commander or the person in charge?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, no one. Just Veselin Sarac, who knew Mr. Naser before the war, I believe. He told us later that he was the man. We didn't hear anything from anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, during your stay at the prison, how many times did you see this person who called himself Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber: What was the occasion of the first time that you saw the person who called himself Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but it was several days after our capture. That was the first time, when this gentleman introduced himself as Naser Oric. And he asked us whether anyone had been touching us or Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond beating us and what had happened to Kukic. We replied that no one was beating us, that Kukic had suffered a stroke. I've told you already why we were in no position to say what had happened. It was for reasons of our personal safety. The next time, the same gentleman came who had previously introduced himself as Naser Oric. He stood outside the cell with the bars, of course. He brought some meat and a knife, which he offered us to eat. The other people took some meat, but I couldn't, because my gums had been torn up and I had wounds inside my mouth. And he asked me why I refused to have any meat. He said: You're afraid of getting poisoned. Look at me. I'll have a piece too. And then he took some meat. I said that I couldn't because I'd caught a cold. There was a window without a glass pane in place. That was the second time. And the third time I saw Mr. Naser was the last night before we were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. I'd like to go back to that first time that you saw the person who called himself Naser Oric. And on that first time, had you already, you and the other prisoners who were there, had you already been beaten in the manner which you testified about previously, with bats or kicked or in any way punched?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the first time Mr. Oric, the person who called himself Mr. Oric was there, did some of the inmates, Mr. Veselin Sarac or Mr. Zoran Bankovic, yourself, did you already have bruises or cuts or possibly signs of injury or maltreatment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't remember about injuries, but we were completely worn out. As for myself, you could see that I had been bleeding from the teeth that had been smashed. There was curdled blood on my chin. Nevenko was seated, because he couldn't even stand up. But there were know visible injuries. They would beat us from the waist up, on the chest, on the back, that sort of thing. They hardly ever hit us or punched us on the face, in order to cause an injury that would have been visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, this person who you said described himself as Mr. Oric, he specifically asked about Mr. Kukic. Is that the Kukic you previously testified about who was killed and then whose body was disposed of?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: On the second time that the person who identified himself as Naser Oric, between the first time and the second time, would it be your testimony that the beatings had continued, the ones that you described previously in the room with the stove?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And for the sake of the record: The physical appearance and the physical state of health of the inmates had deteriorated between the first time Mr. Oric came to see you and the second time that Mr. Oric came to see you; would that be true?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, on the third occasion that this person who identified himself as Naser Oric was in your presence, was that at the cell or was that in another part of the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No. The third time Mr. Oric did not introduce himself, because we knew who he was. It was in that room where the firewood was kept. They summoned all of us into that room, and we all left the cell together. Inside that room, there was Mr. Naser Oric. As far as I remember, and I think my memory still serves me well, I think Kemo and Mrki were also there. I believe that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. I would now like to ask you, and I think I have previously, but once again, you remember giving a statement to the investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor in May 2000; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you gave that statement, did you make a drawing of what the SUP building floor, the floor where the cell was, did you make a drawing of that for the investigator?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: You mean of the building in which we were being kept, the cell, and those rooms that I mentioned? Is that what you have in mind? Or the entire building?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No. Just -- well, the building where -- the floor where your cell was and the different rooms that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you draw the room where the wooden stove was on that design?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to ask the usher to hand out copies of the statement with the attached design that Mr. Radic is referring to. I've been informed that the B/C/S is attached to the statement, and I would like to draw your attention to the design, hand-drawn design, which is at the end. It is currently on Sanction, and the ERN page number is 02030476.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, did you make this design with the assistance of the interpreter and the investigator who took the statement from you in May 2000?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please, could we have it also on the ELMO, also because there are going to be some obvious questions on this sketch here, especially since part of it is in English, part of it is in -- and I want to know also whose handwriting this is, and so on and so forth. So you can lead the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I mean these are obvious questions that arise, and you can go straight to the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you see the sketch before you. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber: Did the interpreter and the investigator assist you in drawing this sketch during the taking of your statement in May 2000?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the writing that is in English on this design, is that writing that was done by someone other than you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I just signed this. You can see my signature here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. So is the writing that is in B/C/S also writing that was done by someone other than you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it clear.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who -- you -- what was your part? Did you draw the sketch, in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was with this lady - I don't know what her name is - in Srebrenica, at the SUP building. We used a piece of perfectly plain paper. I drew this on that piece of paper and I gave it to this lady. And probably this lady or the interpreter back at the SUP building in Milici, once we had returned, drew this and wrote things down in English. They saw me again the next day. I spent three days with them and I signed the drawing. I saw that it was identical to the one I had made, so I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is not the original one that you drew up? In other words, the description of the rooms, the lines. So in other words, if I read you well, what happened was that when you were on the site, you drew up a diagram showing where the rooms were, without writing anything on that diagram except the shapes and the position of the rooms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when we were in Milici, this lady had a PC in front of her. I explained what the building looked like inside and where the rooms were. Probably she entered this information into the computer she was using, and once we were done with the interview, we drove back to Srebrenica. Once we arrived, I took a piece of paper. I drew this and I asked the lady whether she agreed and whether everything was all right. When we entered this room where the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond wood-burning stove used to be, I told her there was an opening in the wall up there, and once she found that, I don't want to seem boastful, but she congratulated me on my sincerity. Because everything I had told her in Milici was exactly the same as she found when we arrived there. And the drawing is a hundred per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but did you do this drawing or did someone else draw it on the basis of what you had described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you just signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just signed it, yes. When the drawing was finished, I signed it, because I realised that it was identical to the one that I had made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, when, for example, in the top left corner you have the shape of a room and the words, "nacelnikova soba," those words were not written by you; they were written by someone else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is the chief's room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but they were written down -- the words were written down by someone else, not by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said it was the chief's room, and I did mark it on my drawing. The distribution of the rooms was the same. Chief's office, the lavatory, and the room where a prisoner from Zenica, as far as I remember, was being kept. I don't think we've got that far yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So basically, all the information that we find on this drawing is based on what you had indicated to this lady?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But is any of the writings, except for your signature there that we can see, is anything of -- any of the writing that you see on this piece of paper yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all mine. It's just that this was copied from the original drawing, and someone added the writing in English on this drawing, which wasn't me, because I can't read or write English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have the original that he drew?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We have this. It was attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to make sure. The lines, the vertical and horizontal lines are made by you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not even. Not on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I had the impression. No. I had the impression that he did these lines and somebody else would make the inscription. My question is: The lines, the vertical and the horizontal lines has been done by you or has been done by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On this paper, on this paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: On this paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these lines - I have to say it again - were drawn -- this same drawing was on a plain piece of paper and it was just transferred, in a manner of speaking, from one piece of paper to another. The lines were the same that I had originally drawn. So the copy is identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Might I say it was scanned. His drawing was eventually scanned. I think that's what ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not in a position to confirm that, Ms. Sellers. And he -- I don't think he's in a position to confirm it either. All right. Go ahead. I mean, so we don't have the original. No. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, is this sketch that we see here an accurate representation of that first floor of the SUP building, or the ground floor, where you were imprisoned in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I assert that it is 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. I would just like to ask you a couple of questions about that. If you would look at -- excuse me. I'd like the usher to be able to then just assist Mr. Radic with the ELMO. Mr. Radic, is that your signature in the lower left-hand corner of the page?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, if you were to move over slightly to the right, does that first square represent how you came into the SUP building with the other prisoners on the 24th of September, the place where you came in? Where would the door of the SUP building be?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you now, just using your hand, walk us to the door from where your cell was.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: This is the entrance, on this side. Then comes the hallway. We would go to the right. And this is our cell. This is the lavatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, would you go back to the room you say was the cell. I notice that it seems to be divided into two pieces.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please explain: What is that first section of the room prior to where you see what appears to be a line and several crosses drawn?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: This was the main door. This was a little hallway, or anteroom. And then you came to an iron door. So the door leads to a small anteroom, and from the anteroom, there is an entrance to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you testified that there were bars in front of your cell, would you just point the Trial Chamber to show where were the bars in front of your cell.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Here. Here, these little lines are the bars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Now, if you would go back out into the hallway, would you show the Trial Chamber where is the room where you've testified that Kemo, Mrki, and others administered beatings and the room in which Mr. Kukic was killed.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: This is the room. So from the cell, you enter the hallway, and then you turn left and enter this room. And from that room, you can go through a door to the adjacent room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, where --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: They are next to the main street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Where in that room, since there is a door with an adjacent room, in which of the rooms were the beatings administered?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: In the first one, here. And I don't know what the adjacent room held, because I never entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is it in that room, that first room that you've shown us where Mr. Kukic was killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, around that room where the wooden stove is, is there a series of windows?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the side of the street. This was the desk. The window was large.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any windows that were internally inside the building that you could look out from the room with the wooden stove into a different part of the building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that. Were there any windows around that room that you could see from the corridor of the building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a small opening in the wall. Just when you enter from the hallway, from the main entrance, on the right. It must have been an admission room for the police, and it was there that the small window was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you show the Trial Chamber the room where the interrogations that you've testified about previously took place.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It's this one, the chief's office. That's the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you please show the Trial Chamber where the stairwell was located. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: As you enter this hallway, you can go to the left or to the right, and you use the stairs to go up. On the right-hand side, the stairs led upstairs; and on the left-hand side was another flight of stairs leading to the basement. So the stairs that led up were rather narrow and were on the right-hand side of the stairwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, moving to the right from the stairs, there appears to be another room. Do you know what this room was used for, if anything?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, I know there was a man held in this room, also a prisoner, from Zenica. He was alone in this room. And perhaps two or three days later, I heard he had been exchanged. So that from then on, we didn't hear or see anyone else in that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see this other prisoner from Zenica while you were imprisoned at the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move this into evidence. I'd ask the registrar, could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just the sketch, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Just the sketch, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P467.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's P467. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Might I ask, will this segment take us to 12.30 or are you intending --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, to 12.30. But please, as we usually do, feel free to ask to stop whenever you like, whenever it's convenient. If you want to stop now, we'll stop now. I mean, to us it doesn't make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd-like to just go to the next segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. And then just regulate yourself, just see when you would like to stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask you to look at Sanctions for a small video clip. There is no sound that is attached to this video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes. I can see from here the reflection on the glass that he has it in front of him as well. Would you tell, please, the witness what you are going to require from him before we start rolling on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Radic, I would like to ask you to look at this video clip that you're seeing, and I will stop it and ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what do you recognise, if anything, in this video clip. And I would say for the Trial Chamber's information and Defence counsel that this is P446. All right. Can we begin, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the building where we were, the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that the building that you've testified was the SUP building, then, where the imprisonment took place, the first one you saw, I'm sorry, not this one that's currently on the screen.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you recognise what this picture, this image, is showing?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the door from the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, please tell the Trial Chamber what this image is showing.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: That's the flight of stairs leading up. That's the small window in that room with the wood-burning stove.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can you see from the corridor, therefore, into the room with the wood-burning stove, if you were standing in the corridor, looking in that direction?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you could see the stove itself, but you could see most of the room, because the stove was in the left corner. That's the other, adjacent room that you could enter from this room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what is the image that's before us now.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Now you see a number of rooms. The first one on the left held this man from Zenica. The second one was the cell where we were detained. And the last, third door on the left, at the end of the corridor, was the lavatory. And those here doors, the first one on the right is the room where we were beaten, the room with the wood-burning stove. I don't know what this other room was. I never entered. This is the window. This is the cell that we were held in. You see there's a door on the left. There is a window in the corner, a very small window.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, would you please tell the Trial Chamber where was the guard positioned in relationship to the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: You mean when he would come in to take us out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When he would come in or when he was guarding you.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: The guard was not with us in the cell. He was there in the room where we were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So where was -- my question is more precisely: When the guard would come to get you, where would he have to come to? To this place with the bars on the door or to the first door with steel?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: From the main hallway, there is a door that leads into an anteroom. So he comes into that anteroom, up to the bars, and then he opens the door, which is also part of the bars, and lets us out, either to the lavatory or to take us out to the beating room, and then he would lock up again after taking out one person; if necessary, he would come back and take another one out; the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I notice that there is a radiator in the back of -- there appears to be a radiator in the back of the room with the cell. Now, was that radiator emitting heat during the time period of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you rather cold as opposed to being at a good temperature while you were in this cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: What do you think? The window had no pane. It was constantly opened. I was almost naked, wearing only shorts, a thin blanket.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So would it be your testimony, trying to explain to the Trial Chamber, that you suffered from coldness, from low temperatures, while in the cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: It was cold, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is this the room that you've testified about where the toilet was?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, was the room in better condition during the time period of your imprisonment than we're seeing it now on our screens?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, is this the hallway or the corridor that you've testified where you would be beaten on the way to the room with the wooden stove?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is this the same corridor where you would be beaten on the way to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Could you just let me see this image again? I'm not quite clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is this the same corridor that led to the bathroom when turning to the left, as it led to the room with the burning stove when one turned from the right from your cell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: This hallway -- I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, was that the corridor that led to the office where the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond police chief was? Not the one you're looking at now. I'm sorry. The previous one that we showed you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are confusing him, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you mind if I just move on, Your Honour? Fine. Thank you. I'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you recognise the image that we see before us now?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: I think that's the hallway leading to the lavatory. That's the entrance. Yes, that's the main entrance, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to ask -- I believe this has already been moved into evidence as a previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This has.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've seen it before already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'll be going into a different area. I think this would be an appropriate time now to take that break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment are because your client hasn't got his earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may just make one observation about timing. This is obviously a very important witness, the sort of witness which we would normally need about as much as time of the Prosecution has. Generally throughout this trial we've been shorter and this is one of the occasions when we'll need about as much time. If the Prosecution can finish today, then there's no problem. Obviously we'd have tomorrow and then there'd time for re-examination. My concern is that my learned friend indicated earlier that she might run over tomorrow. If it's a matter of 15 minutes or so then that's fine, but I certainly couldn't cross-examine this witness in less than three hours, given all the evidence that's been given. This witness has been here once already. It may be onerous for him to stay for the weekend. And so I just raise that matter now because I don't want to be under pressure to finish in less than three hours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will not be under pressure, Mr. Jones. We'll certainly not put you under pressure for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The agreement is as it is. Ms. Sellers, I mean, I don't know what your position is. I will not put you under pressure either. But if you can finish with this witness today it's much better.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will tell Defence counsel now and Your Honours, I think that I might have to run over with this witness. I'd like to go as rapidly as possible. The question will be the nature of the exhibits we're about to use have a time period attached to them. And I believe that that's evidence that the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel should listen to. So if we do run over, meaning continue the direct examination tomorrow, I would certainly hope to finish that direct examination possibly in a half-hour to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but in the meantime, has the witness been alerted to the possibility of having to stay the weekend over?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The witness has not been alerted to that. I mean, we did try -- we did intend to think that we could go just today with Mr. Jones, the Defence counsel, going tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I said, I mean, with important witnesses, we don't like to impose any time-limit. I mean, if it's necessary, we do, but in this particular case, we would impose it on you, not on Mr. Jones at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would regret any further keeping of this witness, who has been extremely generous with his time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move, Ms. Sellers, and try and see if you can finish as quickly as possible. But Mr. Jones will not have less time than he requires, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which basically means that the witness will need -- may need to stay here. So let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I would like now to ask you a couple of questions about Mr. Veselin Sarac, who you've testified was imprisoned with you. Did Veselin Sarac ever, while in the prison, at times leave the cell for purposes other than being beaten or going to the toilet, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: According to my information, Veselin Sarac would leave the cell when Kukic was being taken away. I think I did say that. That was the one time. And I think there was another time he left the cell, but I don't know exactly for how long or when. I found this out later, after we had been exchanged. The second time he left the cell, he went to attend some negotiations to arrange an exchange. He negotiated with Ratko Bjelanovic, who was then, I think, under Naser Oric, and with Cakura. That's all I know about Veselin Sarac leaving the cell, twice, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you just testified that a Mr. Ratko Bjelanovic was under a Mr. Naser Oric. Do you mean that he was working for Naser Oric or would you like to change that testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rade Bjelanovic, he is a Serb, and I believe, or rather, I'm positive that he negotiated to arrange our exchange. He negotiated with Mr. Oric and with Cakura. Veselin told me later, after the exchange, he told me when he returned to the cell, for whatever reason, that he had gone there too to talk to Bjelanovic. That's all I know about Sarac and this time when he was absent from the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like Your Honours now, and the registry, to please, through Sanction, to listen to an audiotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We object to this tape, the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the famous one which we have seen already?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This is a different tape. This is an audiotape that is only -- one has to listen with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. I know the one. Yeah, yeah. Okay, okay, okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've objected because we've requested among other documents and exhibits to inspect the original of this audiotape and we've never been provided with the original. I'd be interested to know firstly whether this is the original tape that the Prosecution has in its possession. And there are other reasons why we object to it, which I can go into, but perhaps shouldn't in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not in front of the witness, yeah. Is this the original or is this a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the tape that was given to us. It's the tape that we have, and we've provided copies, I believe, to the Defence. I'm not in a position to say as to whether it was the original tape that was made from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the IIF form where it states it was not an original and I won't go into the rest of it. So I think the Prosecution knows that they don't have the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed anyway. We've put on record your objection, Mr. Jones, and then we'll see later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which number has it been given already?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's P97, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P97. So it is the one, yes. It is the one. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: While there is some simultaneous translation of this audiotape, we also do have written transcripts. If that can be handed out at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I also just say for the transcript, we object firstly because it's -- the name Naser Oric or NO is placed there, when in fact there's no indication that it's Naser Oric. There's no authentication of voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat that or stress the point, because it's quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We can go into these objections perhaps on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What Your Honours are receiving now are a slightly revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, so I see. It's revised. Well, what we have is P97.1 ^yes, which was exhibited earlier on in the course of this trial. And so this is a revision of that text?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I would invite you to look at the revision. At the same time, we will move to have this revised text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is quite similar to the other one. We've picked with a couple of points that could have been clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I correct the number. It's P97E of the initially provided transcript and not .1E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 97E No, I wouldn't substitute it. I would leave what we have. Have this as well and give it -- and this would be 97.1E, E, 1, and then E and another 1, or .add, add 1. I mean, I don't know. .1E? And this will be P97, Mr. Jones and Ms. Sellers, P97.1E. All right? Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask that the tape be run. Mr. Radic, would you please listen to this audiotape. There's simultaneous translation in English below the screen. I would just ask that you listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: INTERPRETER: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would state that that's the end. I'm sorry. I would state that this is the end of the first segment of the tape. My suggestion would be, should we continue with the second segment, which is approximately 15 minutes long so that this exhibit is finished today and then I would have to proceed with the witness tomorrow in terms of questioning him about this exhibit, one or two other matters, and then we do have a video that we'll show tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think of the -- from what I see here, you may be right. It may take us another 15 minutes to finish the second segment. I don't know, because obviously I haven't heard it before. But I would suggest that we proceed, we finish with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we'll proceed with the questions tomorrow. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the end of the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just to say that my microphone wasn't on. That was the end of the audiotape exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that's all for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Radic, we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 and you will be asked questions on this recording that you've just listened to. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just, I -- I think it's fair to the witness to caution him that the Prosecution--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- will certainly be more than half an hour tomorrow. That means that I will almost certainly not be finished tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, we told you already. I mean, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- what the position is. Mr. Radic, it's very probable that we don't finish with you tomorrow. So if you need to inform your family that it could well be that you'll be staying over the weekend, I think you better prepare them now. Because I don't think we'll finish tomorrow. I'm sorry about that, but we need to finish with your testimony.
